text: Li–S Batteries Correlating Polysulfide Solvation Structure with Electrode Kinetics towards Long-Cycling Lithium–Sulfur Batteries Zheng Li, Li-Peng Hou, Nan Yao, Xi-Yao Li, Zi-Xian Chen, Xiang Chen, Xue-Qiang Zhang, Bo-Quan Li,* and Qiang Zhang* Abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li� S) batteries are promising due to ultrahigh theoretical energy density.
However, their cycling lifespan is crucially affected by the electrode kinetics of lithium polysulfides.
Herein, the polysulfide solvation structure is correlated with polysulfide electrode kinetics towards long-cycling Li� S batteries.

The solvation structure derived from strong solvating power electrolyte induces fast anode kinetics and rapid anode failure, while that derived from weak solvating power electrolyte causes sluggish cathode kinetics and rapid capacity loss.
By contrast, the solvation structure derived from medium solvating power electrolyte balances cathode and anode kinetics and improves the cycling performance of Li� S batteries.
Li� S coin cells with ultra-thin Li anodes and high-Sloading cathodes deliver 146 cycles and a 338 Whkg� 1 pouch cell undergoes stable 30 cycles.
This work clarifies the relationship between polysulfide solvation structure and electrode kinetics and inspires rational electrolyte design for long-cycling Li� S batteries.

Introduction Rechargeable batteries play important roles in the global energy storage system in pursuit of a sustainable and lowcarbon society.[1] Lithium–sulfur (Li� S) batteries are promising next-generation energy storage devices due to their ultrahigh theoretical energy density of 2600 Whkg� 1.[2] Different from the intercalation mechanism in conventional lithium-ion batteries,[3] Li� S batteries follow a dissolutionprecipitation mechanism.[4] Specifically, soluble lithium polysulfide (LiPS) intermediates are generated from elemental sulfur, gradually reduced at the cathode–electrolyte interface, and finally converted into insoluble Li2S during discharge, known as the multi-electron and multi-phase cathodic reactions with a theoretical specific capacity of 1672 mAhg� 1.[5] Meanwhile, Li metal anodes undergo repeated Li stripping and plating during cycling with a theoretical specific capacity of 3860 mAhg� 1 and an ultralow equilibrium potential of � 3.04 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode.
The above electrode processes constitute the basic Li� S chemistry with intrinsic advantages in realizing high energy density far beyond the current Li-ion batteries.

Despite the energy density advantages, the practical application of Li� S batteries is severely restricted by their limited cycling lifespan.[6] The cycling performance of Li� S batteries is crucially affected by the cathode and anode kinetics of LiPSs during charge and discharge.

On one hand, LiPSs act as important intermediates of the solid–liquid– solid conversion reactions and are involved in every electrochemical process at the cathode.[4a] Fast cathode kinetics of LiPSs promises rapid electrochemical conversion and full utilization of the active materials,[7] thus realizing high specific capacity and maintaining high capacity retention.[8] Conversely, sluggish cathode kinetics induces aggravated polarization to result in rapid capacity loss and quick failure of Li� S batteries.[9] On the other hand, the dissolved LiPSs are highly reactive and can chemically react with Li metal once diffused to the anode side.[10] Fast anode kinetics of LiPSs induces severe parasitic reactions on Li metal anodes and rapid depletion of limited Li reservoir.[11] Furthermore, the by-products between LiPSs and Li metal participate in the formation of solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), further deteriorating the transport uniformity of Li ions and exacerbating inhomogeneous Li deposition.[12] Accordingly, fast anode kinetics of LiPSs results in rapid decay of Li metal anodes and limited cycling lifespan of Li� S batteries.[13] Considering the consistent variation of the cathode and anode kinetics, the effects of LiPS electrode kinetics at the cathode and anode on the cycling performance of Li� S batteries are intrinsically contradictory.[14] Therefore, it is extremely necessary to reasonably regulate the LiPS electrode kinetics, specifically, reducing the LiPS anode kinetics without severely deteriorating the LiPS cathode kinetics to construct practical long-cycling Li� S batteries.
The electrode kinetics of LiPSs is tightly bound up with their solvation structure.[15] It has attracted increasing [*] Z.

attention to regulate the LiPS solvation structure through adjusting the solvating power of electrolyte towards optimized electrode kinetics of LiPSs.[16] Electrolytes with weak solvating power, such as high concentration electrolyte (HCE) and localized high concentration electrolyte (LHCE), have been proposed and employed in Li� S batteries.[17] The alteration of the LiPS solvation structure by reducing free solvents suppresses the anode kinetics and thus improves the cycling lifespan of Li� S batteries.[18] However, the sluggish cathode kinetics in HCE and LHCE severely limits the construction of high-energy-density Li� S batteries.[19] On the contrary, electrolytes with strong solvating power have been employed widely in Li� S batteries.

For example, an electrolyte using high-donor-number N-methyl- 2-pyrrolidone (NMP) as additives was proposed and a unique solvation structure was formed with NMP molecules intensively involved in the first solvation sheath of LiPSs.[20] The solvation structure of the NMP-added electrolyte enables fast cathode kinetics and outstanding cathode capacity retention.
However, simultaneously accelerated anode kinetics limits the advantages in practical pouch cells with limited anode excess.

Very recently, a novel electrolyte system with a heterogeneous solvation structure named encapsulating LiPS electrolyte (EPSE) was reported by Zhang and co-workers.[21] The EPSE suppresses the anode kinetics of LiPSs while maintains the cathode kinetics to a certain extent, thus improving the cycling lifespan of Li� S batteries at the pouch cell level.[22] Although the cycling stability of Li� S batteries can be promoted by EPSE, it remains unclear how the LiPS solvation structure influences the electrode kinetics.[23] Therefore, a fundamental understanding of the relationship between the LiPS solvation structure and the electrode kinetics is urgently required for optimized cathode and anode kinetics and rational electrolyte design towards long-cycling Li� S batteries.[24] In this contribution, the LiPS solvation structure is correlated with electrode kinetics to balance the cathode and anode kinetics for long-cycling Li� S batteries.

Concretely, 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)/1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) (1:1, by vol.) mixed solvents with strong solvating power and hydrofluoroether (HFE) with weak solvating power are employed to regulate the solvation structure of LiPSs.
Consequently, a series of double-shell solvation structures of LiPSs are constructed by altering the HFE content to modulate the solvating power of electrolyte.
The solvation structure derived from strong solvating power electrolyte induces fast anode kinetics and rapid failure of Li anodes.
Conversely, the solvation structure derived from weak solvating power electrolyte results in sluggish cathode kinetics and rapid capacity loss due to cathode polarization.
Notably, the solvation structure derived from medium solvating power electrolyte balances the cathode and anode kinetics and therefore improves the cycling performance of working Li� S batteries.
Accordingly, Li� S coin cells with 50 μm Li metal anodes and 4.3 mgcm� 2 S cathodes undergo stable 146 cycles.
Moreover, a 338 Whkg� 1 Li� S pouch cell delivers a prolonged cycling lifespan of 30 cycles with the regulated solvation structure.
Results and Discussion The influence of DME and HFE on the solvating power of electrolyte was first investigated by density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
Models composed of one Li2S8 molecule with two DME, one DME and one HFE, and two HFE were constructed to represent electrolytes with different solvation power (Figure 1A).

The binding energy between Li2S8 and the solvents was selected as an indicator of the solvating power.[25] The binding energy between Li2S8 and two DME is � 2.59 eV and is the highest among the three systems due to the high electron-donating ability and the chelation of DME molecules (Figure 1B).

However, with the substitution of HFE by DME, the systems of Li2S8 with one DME and one HFE as well as Li2S8 with two HFE exhibit lower binding energies of � 2.00 and � 1.36 eV, respectively, indicating the relatively weak solvating power of HFE as expected.
Moreover, the binding energy of Li2S4 with different solvent molecules indicates the same conclusion (Figures S1 and S2).
The solubility of Li2S8 in electrolyte with different contents of HFE was further measured experimentally.
Electrolytes without HFE, with 10%, 20%, or 30% HFE by volume can dissolve 4.3, 2.9, 2.6, and 1.8 M[S] Li2S8 at most, respectively (Figure S3 and Table S1).

Electrolyte with lower solubility of LiPSs generally exhibits weaker solvating power.[16a] Accordingly, the above results suggest that the increase of HFE content in electrolyte reduces the solvating power of electrolyte.
The LiPS solvation structure derived from electrolyte with different solvating power was further revealed by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
Li2S8 was chosen as a typical LiPS.
The MD simulation systems are composed of 1.0 M[S] Li2S8 in DOL and DME (1:1, by vol.) without, with 10%, 20%, or 30% HFE.
The coordination number (CN) of the solvents centered on S8 2�varies in the electrolyte systems with different HFE contents (Figure 1C).
Two plateaus appear in the CN-radius profiles of DME.

Specifically, the first plateau appears at the position from 3.9 Å to 5.5 Å and the second plateau appears at the position larger than 5.5 Å, which are defined as the inner and outer solvation shells, respectively.

It should be noted that the CN of DME in the electrolyte systems with different HFE contents is the same in the inner shell while the CN of DME in the outer shell decreases as the HFE content increases.
On the contrary, HFE only appears in the outer shell and the CN of HFE increases with higher HFE contents.
The number density distributions of DME, DOL, and HFE are depicted in Figures S4 and S5 in detail.
Additionally, DOL in the outer shell shows a similar variation tendency as DME (Figure S6).
Experimentally, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) was employed to investigate the solvation structure of LiPSs.
The 7Li chemical shifts with different HFE contents are similar, indicating similar inner chemical environment of LiPSs, which is in consistent with the results of MD simulation (Figure S7).
To further understand the solvation structure, the number density ratio of HFE and DME was analyzed (Figure 1D).
Taking the position at 8.0 Å for example, the number density ratios of HFE and DME are 0, 0.12, 0.31, Angewandte Chemie Research Articles Angew.

and 0.69 in the electrolyte systems with HFE contents of 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30%, respectively.
Accordingly, a series of double-shell LiPS solvation structures are constructed in the electrolyte systems with different HFE contents.
DME exists in both the inner and the outer shells while HFE only exists in the outer shell due to its weak solvating power (Figures 1E, 1F, and S8).
In addition to Li2S8, the solvation structure of Li2S4 is disclosed in different electrolytes with the same conclusions (Figures S9 and S10).

Both the CN of HFE in the outer shell and the number density ratio of HFE and DME increases as the HFE content increases in the electrolyte systems, and the varied double-shell LiPS solvation structures are generated according to the different solvation power of the electrolytes.

Based on the simulation results, electrolytes with different HFE contents (0%, 10%, 20%, and 30%) were prepared with different solvating power (denoted as strong, mid-strong, mid-weak, and weak, respectively) to realize varied LiPS solvation structures.
The without HFE sample here employs the conventional DOL/DME electrolyte for comparison.
Furthermore, the electrolyte systems are investigated experimentally regarding the electrode kinetics and battery performances.
The solvation structure of LiPSs which derives from strong solvating power electrolyte is briefly denoted as strong solvation structure and other systems are similarly named.
The relationship between the LiPS solvation structure and the anode kinetics was first quantitatively evaluated.
Shuttle current was measured in Li� S coin cells without LiNO3 as an indicator of the anode kinetics regarding LiPSs reacting with Li metal.

Successive decline in shuttle current is observed with reduced solvating power of the electrolyte in the voltage range from 2.34 to 2.40 V, indicating suppressed parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li metal and reduced LiPS anode kinetics with weak solvation structure (Figure 2A).
Coulombic efficiency (CE) was further analyzed in Li� S coin cells without LiNO3 to determine the anode kinetics of LiPSs.
The initial CE of the cells with strong, mid-strong, mid-weak, and weak solvation structures is 38.2%, 45.4%, 67.1%, and 81.8%, respectively, which is consistent with the shuttle current tests.
Therefore, the LiPS anode kinetics reduces as the solvating power for the LiPS solvation structure decreases (Figure 2B).
The effect of reduced anode kinetics was further proved by post analyses on the cycled Li� S cells.

According to the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images, Li deposition in the electrolyte with the strong solvation structure is loose and porous after 5 cycles, and dendritic Li is observed apparently (Figures 2C and S11).
However, as the solvating power reduces, the deposited Li becomes denser and smoother.
Especially, the weak solvation structure derives chunky deposited Li that plies up densely with a diameter of about 20 μm.
Furthermore, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was employed to investigate the SEI composition.
The S content in SEI decreases in turn for strong (4.18%), mid-strong (2.79%), mid-weak (1.74%), and weak (1.41%) solvation structures (Figure 2D).
The existing forms of S are similar with the varied solvation structures, including both high-valence species (Li2SO4 and Li2SO3) and low-valence species (Li2S, Li2S2, and LiPSs) (Figure S12).

In addition, the F atomic content and species distribution in SEI derived from different solvation structures are similar (Figures S13 and S14), and the reductive stability of HFE is rather high on Li metal anodes verified by cyclic voltammetry (CV) profiles (Figure S15).
Therefore, HFE does not participate in SEI formation and the electrode kinetic differences are mainly attributed to the different solvation structures.
Briefly, stronger solvation structure induces faster LiPS anode kinetics.
Weak solvation structure suppresses the parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li metal and improves the stability of Li metal anodes (Figures 2E and 2F).
On the other hand, the cathode kinetics of LiPSs with different solvation structures was evaluated.
First, the overall cathode kinetics was tested via CV in Li j Li2S8 cells with a carbon paper (CP) cathode and different electrolytes containing Li2S8.
The CV profiles were collected in a voltage window of 1.7–2.8 V at a scan rate of 0.5 mVs� 1.
Two reduction peaks and one oxidation peak are displayed and denoted as peak R1, R2, and O, respectively (Figure 3A).
Peak R1 appears at 2.02, 2.01, 1.97, and 1.78 V with strong, mid-strong, mid-weak, and weak solvation structures, respectively.
Peak R2 shows the same tendency as peak R1, which appears at 2.30, 2.25, 2.18, and 2.16 V, respectively.
On the contrary, peak O exhibits a right shift as the solvating power reduces, appearing at 2.45, 2.47, 2.50, and 2.53 V, respectively.
All the shifts of peak R1, R2, and O indicate increased voltage polarization corresponding to retarded redox kinetics with decreased solvating power for the solvation structures.
The peak currents were further obtained from the CV profiles.
When the solvation structure varies from strong to weak, the peak current decreases from 0.75 to 0.35 mAcm� 2 for peak R1 and from 1.5 to 0.38 mAcm� 2 for peak R2, respectively (Figure 3B).
The increased voltage polarization and decreased peak currents suggest that weak solvation structure induces sluggish cathode kinetics of LiPSs.
Considering the multiphase conversion reactions of the cathode processes, the liquid–liquid and liquid–solid conversion kinetics was separately investigated.
The liquid– liquid conversion kinetics between dissolved LiPSs was quantitatively evaluated by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of Li2S6 symmetric cells.
The Li2S6 symmetric cells were assembled with two CP electrodes and electrolytes containing Li2S6.

Similar results are exhibited regarding the contact resistance (Rcon) in the high-frequency region while the charge transfer resistance (Rct) sharply increases from strong to weak solvation structures in the lowfrequency region (Figure 3C).[26] The increased Rct indicates sluggish liquid–liquid conversion kinetics as the solvating power reduces.
Meanwhile, the liquid–solid conversion kinetics regarding the transition from LiPSs to Li2S was investigated by chronoamperometric nucleation tests in Lij Li2S8 cells.
As depicted in Figure 3D, the current response curves at 2.05 V are presented and the Li2S deposition capacities are obtained according to the integrated area.

The solvation structures from strong to weak afford decreased Li2S deposition capacities of 161, 98, 89, and 71 mAhg� 1, respectively, indicating inhibited Li2S deposition with the weak solvation structure.
Therefore, the cathode kinetics becomes more sluggish regarding the liquid–liquid and liquid–solid conversion processes as the solvating power reduces.
The solvation structure derived from high solvating power electrolyte promises favorable LiPS cathode kinetics.
To gain deeper insights into the cathode kinetics of LiPSs, the polarization of the cathode redox reactions was decoupled by galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT).

were assembled and discharged galvanostatically at 0.1 C (1 C=1672 mAg� 1) with a ten-minute discharge and a twohour rest in each GITT step.

The difference between the working voltage and the equilibrium voltage represents the total voltage polarization including activation polarization (ηact), ohmic polarization (ηohm), and concentration polarization (ηcon).
Specifically, as shown in Figure S16, the instant voltage recovery corresponds to the sum of ηact and ηohm because they both exist only when there is an applied current.
On the contrary, the gradual voltage recovery over time represents ηcon corresponding to the hysteretic diffusion of the reactive species.
In order to decouple ηact and ηohm, EIS was further conducted to obtain the ohmic resistance, and ηohm can be obtained by multiplying the ohmic resistance and the applied current.

According to the GITT results depicted in Figure S17, the Li� S cells with different LiPS solvation structures exhibit similar equilibrium voltages to indicate unchanged thermodynamics despite the varied LiPS solvation structures.

However, the working voltage decreases sharply corresponding to large polarization and retarded cathode kinetics as the solvating power reduces, especially for the cells with weak solvation structure.
The total polarization is exhibited in Figure 4A by comparing the equilibrium and the working voltages of the cells.
According to the EIS results, the ohmic resistance is so low that the variation of ηohm can be reasonably neglected (Figures S18, S19 and Table S2).
Therefore, ηohm is considered to be a constant over the whole discharge process.

Through further decoupling the total polarization, it is found that ηcon exhibits a slight increase from strong to weak solvation structures to indicate a minor limitation on mass transfer (Figure 4B).
On the contrary, ηact exhibits a sharp increase, especially for the cells with the weak solvation structure and reaches up to 362 mV at the specific capacity of 336 mAhg� 1 (Figure 4C).
The enormous ηact appears at the transition region between the first and the second plateau, which possibly originates from the obstruction of Li2S nucleation and deposition.

Decoupled polarization at the specific capacity of 308 mAhg� 1 is further depicted in Figure 4D. ηcon increases from 55 to 81 mV while ηact increases from 38 to 223 mV with the solvation structure changing from strong to weak.
The percentage of ηact in the total polarization boosts sharply from 40.2% to 72.5%, demonstrating that the increase of ηact is the decisive factor for the sluggish cathode kinetics.

Therefore, the strong solvation structure of LiPSs promotes the cathode kinetics of LiPSs while the weak solvation structure induces sluggish cathode kinetics and raises severe activation polarization during the phase conversion processes (Figures 4E and 4F).

To summarize, fast anode kinetics from the strong solvation structure and sluggish cathode kinetics from the weak solvation structure are both suggested to limit the cycling stability of Li� S batteries.
An optimized solvation structure derived from medium solvating power electrolyte is expected to balance the cathode and anode kinetics and achieve long-cycling Li� S batteries.
The effect of different solvation structures in Li� S full cells was evaluated.
Li� S coin cells were assembled with an ultrathin Li anode of 50 μm in thickness, a high-S-loading cathode of 4.3 mgcm� 2, and an electrolyte to S (E/S) ratio of 6.1 μLmg� 1.
As expected, the Li� S coin cell with the strong solvation structure exhibits the most excellent rate performance.
Not only a high specific capacity of 1040 mAhg� 1 is delivered at 0.1 C, but also a satisfactory specific capacity of 874 mAhg� 1 can be achieved at a high rate of 0.5 C (Figure 5A).

The rate performance of the Li� S coin cells proves fast cathode kinetics with strong solvation structure.
The cycling performance of the Li� S coin cells was further evaluated at 0.1 C.

The CE follows the order from low to high as the solvating power for the solvation structure reduces, dropping down to 90% at the 38th, 65th, and 106th cycle with strong, mid-strong, and mid-weak solvation structures, respectively (Figures 5C and S21).

Moreover, the Li� S coin cell with the mid-weak solvation structure delivers an ultra-long cycling lifespan of 146 cycles with an initial specific capacity of 887 mAhg� 1 and a capacity retention of 78.5% due to the balanced cathode and anode kinetics.
The cycling performance of the coin cell with the mid-weak solvation structure is superior compared with other recent advanced works (Table S3).
Similarly, the Li� S coin cell with the mid-strong solvation structure delivers a cycling lifespan of 122 cycles with an initial specific capacity of 889 mAhg� 1 and a capacity retention of 66.5%.

In comparison, the Li� S coin cell with the strong solvation structure exhibits a rapid drop in capacity after 30 cycles and a low capacity retention of 63.7% after 60 cycles, despite the highest initial specific capacity of 1013 mAhg� 1.
The low capacity retention originates from the serious parasitic reactions between Li metal and LiPSs owning to the fast anode kinetics.

Additionally, the Li� S coin cell with the weak solvation structure exhibits a cliff-like capacity drop after 30 cycles with the lowest initial specific capacity of 778 mAhg� 1 due to the sluggish cathode kinetics.
Specifically, the voltage–specific capacity profiles at the 5th cycle are presented in Figure 5D.
The voltage polarization, especially at the transition region between the first and the second plateau, increases successively as the solvating power reduces.

Furthermore, according to the voltage–specific capacity profiles at the 40th cycle presented in Figures 5E and S22, the Li� S coin cell with the mid-strong or the mid-weak solvation structure displays a stable second discharge plateau voltage owning to suppressed anode kinetics and unrestricted cathode kinetics.
However, the Li� S coin cell with the strong solvation structure displays a sloping second discharge plateau with large voltage polarization.
The large voltage polarization is attributed to Li anode failure caused by the fast anode kinetics of LiPSs, which induces rapid depletion of limited Li reservoir and accumulated inactive Li.

Additionally, the Li� S coin cell with the weak solvation structure displays a very limited discharge capacity without the second discharge plateau owning to the large voltage polarization afforded by the sluggish cathode kinetics.

The above results clearly verify the effect of the different solvation structures on the cycling performance of Li� S batteries and the necessity of balancing the cathode and anode kinetics to achieve long-cycling Li� S batteries.

To further verify the relationship between the solvation structure and the electrode kinetics to achieve long-cycling Li� S batteries under practical conditions, Li� S pouch cells were assembled and evaluated.
The pouch cells were 4×7 cm2 in size with stacks of double-layer Li anodes and S cathodes (Figure 6A).
The thickness of the Li anode is 75 μm and the areal S loading of S cathodes is 7.4 mgcm� 2 for a single side.
The pouch cells were cycled at 0.05 C with a low E/S ratio of 3.5 ggS � 1.

The Li� S pouch cell with the medium solvation structure delivers a prolonged cycling lifespan of 30 cycles with an initial energy density of 338 Whkg� 1 based on the total mass of the whole pouch cell (Table S4).
The cycling performance of the pouch cell with the medium solvation structure is superior compared with other recent advanced works (Table S5).

reduced cycling lifespan of only 19 cycles, and that with the weak solvation structure only cycles normally for the first cycle (Figure 6B).

Specifically, the discharge profiles with the strong and the medium solvation structures at the 2nd cycle both display two typical discharge plateaus while that with the weak solvation structure displays only one short discharge plateau due to the blocked cathode kinetics (Figure 6C).

At the 20th cycle, the pouch cell with the medium solvation structure affords a complete second discharge plateau despite enlarged voltage polarization and delivers a high specific capacity of 999 mAhg� 1.

Conversely, the pouch cell with the strong solvation structure displays a sloping and short second discharge plateau due to the destructed Li anodes rendered by the fast LiPS anode kinetics (Figure 6D).
Consequently, only the Li� S pouch cell with the medium solvation structure possesses moderate electrode kinetics of both the cathode and the anode and thus achieves a prolonged cycling lifespan.

Balancing the cathode and anode kinetics through regulating the solvating power of the LiPS solvation structure is validated to be effective in realizing high-energy-density and long-cycling Li� S pouch cells.
Conclusion In summary, the LiPS solvation structure is correlated with electrode kinetics to balance the cathode and anode kinetics for achieving long-cycling Li� S batteries.
The strong solvation structure induces fast anode kinetics and rapid failure of Li anodes.
Conversely, the weak solvation structure results in sluggish cathode kinetics and rapid capacity loss.
The medium solvation structure balances the cathode and anode kinetics and improves the cycling performance of working Li� S batteries.
Accordingly, Li� S coin cells with 50 μm Li metal anodes and 4.3 mgcm� 2 S cathodes deliver 146 cycles.
Li� S pouch cells with superior energy density up to 338 Whkg� 1 undergo over 30 cycles with the regulated solvation structure.

This work clarifies the relationship between the LiPS solvation structure and the electrode kinetics, proposes a rational electrolyte designing methodology for electrode kinetic regulation, and inspires further comprehension on the LiPS solvation structure to achieve long-cycling practical Li� S batteries.

SUPPORTING INFORMATION 1 1.
Experimental Section 1.1.

Raw materials Lithium (Li) metal foils were purchased from China Energy Lithium Co., Ltd. 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, DoDoChem), 1,3- dioxolane (DOL, DoDoChem), 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropylether (HFE, TCI), LiNO3 (Aladdin), lithium bis- (trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI, DoDoChem), Li2S (Alfa), elemental sulfur (S8, Alfa), aluminum (Al) foils, polypropylene (PP) membranes (Celgard 2400), carbon nanotubes (CNTs, Cnano), poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF, HSV-300), and N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP, Aladdin) were used as purchased without further purification. 1.2.

Preparation of electrolytes A mixture of DOL/DME (1:1, by vol.) or mixed with 10%, 20% or 30% HFE by volume was first prepared. 1.0 M LiTFSI was then dissolved in the above four mixed solvents with 2 wt.% LiNO3 to obtain electrolytes with different solvating power.
To prepare the electrolyte with Li2S8 or Li2S6, Li2S and S8 were mixed with a molar ratio of 8:7 or 8:5, respectively, in the above electrolytes with a concentration of 1.0 M[S].
All the electrolytes were prepared in an argon-filled glove box with O2 and H2O contents below 0.1 ppm. 1.3.
Preparation of sulfur cathodes Sulfur/CNT (S/CNT) composite was prepared through ball-milling.
A mixture of CNT and S8 (3:7, by wt.) was ball-milled with PVDF binders at a weight ratio of 9:1 in NMP to form a homogeneous slurry.
The slurry was then cast onto an Al foil and dried at 60°C for 12 h to obtain S cathodes.
The S cathodes were punched into disks with a diameter of 13.0 mm and the areal S loading was 1.3 or 4.3 mg cm−2 for electrochemical measurements. 1.4.

Evaluation on anode kinetics For the measurements of anode kinetics, lithium–sulfur (Li–S) cells were assembled with 600 μm Li anodes (16.0 mm in diameter), 1.3 mg cm−2 S cathodes, PP separators (19.0 mm in diameter), and 25 μL electrolyte without LiNO3.
The Li–S cells were tested on a Neware battery cycler (CT-4008T, Shenzhen, China) at room temperature.
For the shuttle current tests, the Li–S cells were firstly galvanostatically charged to 2.90 V and then discharged to 2.40, 2.39, 2.38, 2.37, 2.36, 2.35, and 2.34 V step by step.
At each voltage step, the cells were kept potentiostatically for 1.0 h.
The shuttle current was determined by the steady-state current at different potentiostatic voltages.
Furthermore, the Li–S cells were cycled at 0.1 C (1 C = 1672 mA g−1) with a voltage range of 1.70– 2.60 V for Coulombic efficiency (CE) evaluation and further analyses. 1.5.

Evaluation on cathode kinetics For the overall cathode kinetic evaluation, Li | Li2S8 cells were assembled with 600 μm Li anodes (16.0 mm in diameter), carbon paper (CP) cathodes (13.0 mm in diameter), PP separators (19.0 mm in diameter), and 25 μL electrolyte with 1.0 M[S] Li2S8.
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed with a scan rate of 0.5 mV s−1 and a voltage window of 1.70–2.80 V.

For the liquid–liquid cathode kinetic evaluation, Li2S6 symmetric cells were assembled with CP electrodes (both 13.0 mm in diameter), PP separators (19.0 mm in diameter), and 40 μL electrolyte with 1.0 M[S] Li2S6.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed at the open circuit voltage with a sinusoidal voltage amplitude of 10 mV and a frequency range from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz.
For the liquid–solid cathode kinetic evaluation, chronoamperometric nucleation tests were conducted.
The Li | Li2S8 cells were discharged galvanostatically at 0.117 mA to 2.06 V and then potentiostically discharged at 2.05 V.
All the above tests were conducted on a Solartron 1470E electrochemical workstation.
For the decoupling of cathode kinetics, galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) was conducted.
Li–S cells were assembled with 50 μm Li anodes (15.0 mm in diameter), 4.3 mg cm−2 S cathodes, PP separators (19.0 mm in diameter), and 35 μL electrolyte without lithium polysulfides.
The as-assembled cells were discharged at 0.1 C with a ten-minute discharge and a two-hour rest at each step between 1.70 and 2.60 V on the Neware battery cycler.

To obtain the ohmic resistance, EIS was performed at the open circuit voltage before the GITT test with a sinusoidal voltage amplitude of 10 mV and a frequency range from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz on the Solartron 1470E electrochemical workstation. 1.6.
Material characterization Li metal anodes after 5 cycles were disassembled from Li–S cells, washed for 3 times with DME to remove residual electrolyte and dried in the glove box thoroughly.
The morphology was characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM 7401F, JEOL Ltd., Japan) operated at 3.0 kV.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) experiments were carried out on a scanning X-ray microprobe (Quantera SXM, ULVAC-PHI.
INC) operated at 250 kV with monochromated Al Kα radiation as the X-ray source. 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra (JNM-ECA600) were recorded at 233.2 MHz at room temperature. 1.7.
Li–S full cell assembly and battery performance evaluation The Li–S full cell performances were evaluated using standard 2032 coin-type cells.

The Li–S coin cells were assembled with ultrathin Li anodes of 50 μm (15.0 mm in diameter, 43% excess in theory), high-S-loading cathodes of 4.3 mg cm−2, PP separators (19.0 mm in diameter), and 35 μL electrolyte (electrolyte to S (E/S) ratio of 6.1 μL mg−1).

The cells were galvanostatically cycled with a voltage range of 1.70–2.60 V at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 C for rate performance evaluation and at 0.1 C for cycling performance evaluation on the Neware battery cycler.
SUPPORTING INFORMATION 2 For Li–S pouch cell evaluation, the S/CNT slurry prepared in section 1.3. was double-side coated on Al foils and dried at 60°C for 12 h.
Then, S cathodes with a single-side areal S loading of 7.4 mg cm−2 were cut into a size of 4 × 7 cm2.
The thickness of Li metal anodes was 75 μm on a single side and 4 × 7 cm2 in size (25% excess in theory).
The pouch cells were assembled with stacks of PP separators, double-side Li metal anodes, and double-side S cathodes in a dry room with a dew point below −40°C.
A low E/S ratio of 3.5 g gS−1 was employed.
The pouch cells were tested at 0.05 C (1 C = 1000 mA g−1) with a voltage range of 1.70–2.55 V on the Neware battery cycler.
The energy density was calculated based on the total mass of the pouch cell and the details are listed in Table S3. 1.8.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculation The DFT calculations were carried out in Gaussian (G16) program[1] with Becke’s three-parameter hybrid method using the Lee– Yang–Parr correlation functional (B3LYP)[2] at 6-311+G(d,p) level.
The solvation effect was considered with the universal solvation model of SMD[3] employing parameters of DME.

The binding energy (Eb) between a lithium polysulfide (LiPS, Li2S8 or Li2S4) and solvents (DME and/or HFE) was defined as follows: Eb = Ecluster – (ELiPS + Esolvents) where Ecluster and ELiPS represent the total energy of the cluster and LiPS, respectively.
Esolvents is the total energy of two DME solvents, one DME solvent and one HFE solvent, or two HFE solvents that coordinate with LiPS. 1.9.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation MD simulations were conducted by the Large Scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) code.[4] Four models were constructed to simulate electrolytes without or with 10%, 20%, or 30% HFE by volume for Li2S8 or Li2S4 systems, respectively, and the detailed compositions of these models are listed in Tables S6.

The force field parameters for solvents were generated by the LigParGen web server[5] except that restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) atomic partial charges were assigned to each atom, which was obtained based on electrostatic potential (ESP) charges using the Multiwfn program.[6] The parameters for Li+, TFSI−, S82−, and S42− were obtained from Jensen et al.,[7] Koddermann et al.,[8] and Rajput et al.,[9] respectively.

The initial atomic coordinates were generated with Packing Optimization for Molecular Dynamics Simulations (Packmol) program.[10] Each system was first equilibrated in the NPT ensemble using the Parrinello–Rahman barostat for 2 ns to maintain a temperature of 298 K and a pressure of 1 atm with time constants of 0.1 and 1 ps, respectively.[11] After that, the electrolytes were heated from 298 K to 420 K within 2 ns, and maintained at 420 K for 4 ns, followed by annealing from 420 K to 298 K within 2 ns.
Subsequently, all systems were equilibrated at 298 K in the NPT ensemble for another 4 ns.
A 12 ns production run was finally conducted in the NVT ensemble under Nose–Hoover thermostat.[12] Only the final 5 ns trajectory was sampled for the analysis of solvation structures.
The solvation structures were visualized by VESTA.[13]
